L16: > Abstract:To provide robustness of distributed model predictive control (DMPC), this work proposes a robust DMPC formulation for discrete-time linear systems subject to unknown-but-bounded disturbances. Taking advantage of the structure of certain classes of distributed systems seen in applications with interagent coupling like vehicle platooning, a novel robust DMPC is formulated.
L17: The proposed approach is characterised by separable terminal costs and locally robust terminal sets, with the latter sets adaptively estimated in the online optimisation problem. A constraint tightening approach based on a set-membership approach is used to guarantee constraint satisfaction for coupled subsystems in the presence of disturbances. Under this formulation, the closed-loop system is shown to be recursively feasible and input-to-state stable.
L18: To aid in the deployment of the proposed robust DMPC, a possible synthesis method and design conditions for practical implementation are presented. Finally, simulation results with a mass-spring-damper system are provided to demonstrate the proposed robust DMPC.

L134: ## Abstract
L135: In this study, a novel output feedback model predictive control based on ellipsoidal set-membership state estimation is proposed for systems with unknown but bounded external disturbances. The set-membership state estimation is utilised to estimate the current system states for the optimisation of model predictive control such that the actual states are not required. Ellipsoidal set-membership estimation guarantees that the real system state lies in the ellipsoid originated from the estimated state.
L136: The control inputs computed by solving the optimisation problem recursively regulate the system state to converge to a domain containing the origin. All the quadratic matrix inequality conditions are conservatively approximated as linear matrix inequality conditions such that the optimisation problems can be solved by using semi-definite programming.
L137: System constraints are analysed over all the prediction horizon and transformed into linear matrix inequalities for the direct incorporation into the optimisation. Simulation examples demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
L138: ## 1 Introduction
L139: Model predictive control (MPC) is an effective strategy to deal with multi-variable constrained control problems using different optimal control methods [【20†1】, 【21†2】]. In MPC, the model of the controlled system is used to predict the future system behaviours over a finite horizon. The optimal control sequence is obtained through solving an optimisation problem, that is to choose the sequence that minimises a cost function.
L140: Only the first control action of the obtained sequence is implemented, and this procedure is repeated in every sampling period [【22†3】]. MPC has advantages on the simplicity of the algorithm and the flexibility to handle hard constraints on states and inputs [【20†1】, 【22†3】, 【23†4】].
L141: However, many previous works on MPC assume that system states are available, which usually cannot be achieved in real industrial processes [【24†5】–【25†7】]. Intuitively, the most common approach is to estimate the system states. Different state estimation approaches, e.g. Kalman filter and Luenberger observer, have already been applied in the literature [【26†8】–【27†10】].
L142: Instead of applying these conventional state estimators, some dynamic output feedback methods by including the estimation error constraints in the main optimisation problem have been proposed in [【28†11】, 【29†12】].

L28@P0: We address the general problem of multiple target localization and pursuit using measurements of the
L29@P0: ranges from the targets to a set of autonomous pursuing vehicles, referred to as trackers. We develop
L30@P0: a general framework for targets with models exhibiting uncertainty in the initial state, process, and
L31@P0: measurement noise. The main objective is to compute optimal motions for the trackers that maximize
L32@P0: the range-based information available for target localization and at the same time yield good target
L33@P0: pursuit performance. The solution proposed is rooted in an estimation-theoretical setting that involves
L34@P0: the computation of an appropriately defined Bayesian Fisher Information Matrix (FIM). The inverse of
L35@P0: the latter yields a posterior Cramér–Rao Lower Bound (CRLB) on the covariance of the targets’ state
L36@P0: estimation errors that can be possibly achieved with any estimator. Using the FIM, sufficient conditions
L37@P0: on the trackers’ motions are derived for the ideal relative geometry between the trackers and the
L38@P0: targets for which the range information acquired is maximal. This allows for an intuitive understanding
L39@P0: of the types of ideal tracker trajectories. To deal with realistic constraints on the trackers’ motions
L40@P0: and the requirement that the trackers pursue the targets, we then propose a model predictive control
L41@P0: (MPC) framework for optimal tracker motion generation with a view to maximizing the predicted
L42@P0: range information for target localization while taking explicitly into account the trackers’ dynamics,
L43@P0: strict constraints on the trackers’ states and inputs, and prior knowledge about the targets’ states. The
L44@P0: efficacy of the MPC is assessed in simulation through the help of representative examples motivated
L45@P0: by operational scenarios involving single and multiple targets and trackers.

L47@P0: 1. Introduction
L48@P0: The problem of target localization and pursuit has received
L49@P0: widespread attention due to its importance in a vast number of
L50@P0: applications in the areas of marine science, surveillance and reconnaissance, search-and-rescue, and military operations, see [1–
L51@P0: 4]. In the literature, localization usually refers to the problem
L52@P0: of finding the location of an unknown stationary target, while

L62@P0: tracking refers to the task of estimating the trajectory of a moving
L63@P0: target. In the present paper, localization includes both tasks. Pursuit, in what follows, has the more control-oriented meaning of
L64@P0: ensuring that in the course of their motion the entities in charge
L65@P0: of estimating the trajectories of the targets stay in pre-defined
L66@P0: neighborhoods of the targets. In this context, target pursuit is a
L67@P0: secondary task that aims to enhance the ‘‘visibility’’ of the targets
L68@P0: so as to yield better quality of the information available for target
L69@P0: localization. In the present paper, this information consists of
L70@P0: measurements of the ranges between the trackers and the targets.
L71@P0: The simplest and most classical problem of range-based target
L72@P0: localization is that of computing the position of a single fixed
L73@P0: target using a network of fixed sensors equipped with rangemeasuring devices. A fundamental problem arising in this context
L74@P0: is that of deciding on the number of sensors and how to best place
L75@P0: them so that the position of the target can be uniquely estimated
L76@P0: with a desired level of accuracy (optimal sensor placement). A

L79@P1: solution to this problem can be obtained by adopting an estimation theoretical framework that involves the computation of
L80@P1: an appropriately defined Fisher information matrix (FIM). See for
L81@P1: example [5–7] for a discussion of these issues. See also [8] for
L82@P1: optimal sensor placement solutions in the case of multiple static
L83@P1: targets and sensors.
L84@P1: In recent years, there has been growing interest in exploiting
L85@P1: the use of single or multiple mobile sensors (called trackers) for
L86@P1: target localization, focusing on applications with unmanned aerial
L87@P1: vehicles (UAVs) and autonomous marine vehicles (AMVs), see
L88@P1: for example [1,9–13] and the references therein. In this setup,
L89@P1: the trackers carry range measuring devices to acquire successive
L90@P1: ranges to the targets of interest and use the range information
L91@P1: to estimate the state of each target. Obviously, this approach has
L92@P1: many advantages when compared with the traditional method
L93@P1: of using a fixed sensor network. First, thanks to the mobility
L94@P1: of the trackers, ranges can be acquired from a large number
L95@P1: of positions relative to each target, thus potentially providing
L96@P1: more information for target localization [9]. Second, the visibility
L97@P1: of the targets can be facilitated by controlling the trackers to
L98@P1: be close to the targets. In the marine environment the use of
L99@P1: trackers in the form of AMVs avoids the cumbersome and costly
L100@P1: deployment of long baseline (LBL) systems that are classically
L101@P1: used in underwater target localization.
L102@P1: This, however leads to the challenging problem of how to plan
L103@P1: the motion of the trackers such that their maneuvers ensure that
L104@P1: the measured ranges from the trackers to the targets yield, in
L105@P1: a well defined mathematical sense, the information needed to
L106@P1: estimate the position of the target with a given level of accuracy
L107@P1: through the use of an appropriately designed estimator. Technically, the answer to this problem should provide conditions on
L108@P1: the motions of trackers that yield target motion observability,
L109@P1: given measurements of the ranges between trackers and targets.
L110@P1: A classical approach to this problem reported in the literature is
L111@P1: to utilize tools from observability analysis, see for example [12,
L112@P1: 14–17] and references therein. For instance, in [14], the author
L113@P1: shows that it is impossible to observe a target moving at a constant velocity vector if the tracker (observer) moves at a constant
L114@P1: velocity as well. However, if the tracker’s trajectory is composed
L115@P1: of at least two straight line segments with different orientations,
L116@P1: the target’s motion is observable if certain conditions on the
L117@P1: bearing between the tracker and the target are satisfied. This
L118@P1: analysis is further investigated in [15] where the trajectory of the
L119@P1: tracker is considered to be smooth. In [16], the author analyzes
L120@P1: the relative motion between the target and tracker using observability rank condition given in the work of [18]. Recent work
L121@P1: in [17] provides a set of necessary and sufficient conditions on
L122@P1: the motions of one or two trackers under which different type’s of
L123@P1: target’s motions are observable. In general, the above approaches
L124@P1: provide conditions on the tracker’s trajectories that yield target state observability. However, these are essentially qualitative
L125@P1: result that do not provide a good measure of how observable
L126@P1: the target motions, a key requisite for adequate tracker motion
L127@P1: planning.
L128@P1: A quantitative approach to motion planning can be derived
L129@P1: using the celebrated Fisher Information Matrix (FIM), as a means
L130@P1: to quantify the amount of information that range measurements
L131@P1: carry about the motions of a target. Using this approach, the
L132@P1: target localization problem is converted into that of finding conditions on the trackers’ trajectories that maximize range-related
L133@P1: information available to estimate the target’s state. We recall
L134@P1: that in an estimation theoretical framework, the inverse of the
L135@P1: FIM yields a lower bound (the celebrated Cramér–Rao lower
L136@P1: bound, abbreviated CRLB) on the covariance of the target’s state
L137@P1: estimation error that can possibly be achieved with any practical
L138@P1: estimator [4,19,20]. In the context of range-based target localization, the CRLB is mostly used to access the performance that
L139@P1: can be achieved with target state estimators [4,21]. A number
L140@P1: of studies that exploit the use of the FIM for tracker motion
L141@P1: planning have been published in the literature, see [9,13,22] and
L142@P1: the reference therein for the case of one tracker one target.
L143@P1: More recently, similar tools have been used to tackle the tracker
L144@P1: motion planning problem in the case of multiple tracker–multiple
L145@P1: target configurations [13]. Notice, however that in [13,22] the
L146@P1: authors resort to the use of the so-called parametric FIM. In
L147@P1: this context, the targets evolve in a deterministic manner and
L148@P1: the initial conditions of the targets are viewed as parameters to
L149@P1: be estimated. As such, the work eschews the far more realistic
L150@P1: case where the initial state of the targets (prior information) is
L151@P1: described by a random variable that captures the uncertainty in
L152@P1: their location, a fact that mandates the use of so-called Bayesian
L153@P1: FIM and the computation of posterior CRLBs [19], explained later
L154@P1: in the present paper. Most approaches to target localization, including those reported in [13,22], also fail to address explicitly the
L155@P1: constraints introduced by the limitations in the maneuverability
L156@P1: of the trackers. In addition, the guidance law proposed in [13,22]
L157@P1: for the trackers is based on the assumption that the motions
L158@P1: of the targets are known in advance, which is unrealistic in the
L159@P1: context of target localization. Still, the results in [13] are valuable
L160@P1: in terms of understanding at an intuitive level, what kinds of
L161@P1: optimal tracker trajectories are suited to selected types of target
L162@P1: motion patterns.
L163@P1: Motivated by the above considerations, in the present paper
L164@P1: we provide an answer to the question of ‘‘how to plan optimal
L165@P1: motions’’ for a set of trackers so as to maximize the range information available to localize and pursue multiple unknown targets
L166@P1: by exploiting the properties of an appropriately defined Bayesian
L167@P1: FIM. Specifically, the main contributions of the paper include the
L168@P1: following:
L169@P1: (i) We construct a Bayesian FIM using the range measurements from multiple trackers to multiple targets as a
L170@P1: means to quantify the range information for the estimation of targets’ states. The formalism adopted allows for
L171@P1: the study of problems far more appropriate and realistic
L172@P1: than those addressed in [13]. First, we consider a more
L173@P1: general scenario (later denoted Scenario B) where the velocity vectors of the targets are considered to be unknown
L174@P1: and must be estimated. Second, the motion of targets are
L175@P1: considered to be a dynamical system with given prior
L176@P1: information, allowing us to incorporate explicitly the prior
L177@P1: knowledge of the targets’ states. Third, the FIM in the
L178@P1: current paper is the Bayesian FIM [19] which is more
L179@P1: suitable and appropriate for the problem considered than
L180@P1: the parametric FIM studied in [13]. The Bayesian FIM takes
L181@P1: into account the dynamics of the trackers and the targets
L182@P1: systematically and is computed sequentially, making its
L183@P1: computation simpler, clean and more transparent than the
L184@P1: method adopted in [13]. Fourth, the depths of the trackers
L185@P1: and targets are explicitly taken into account. Lastly, we
L186@P1: derive sufficient conditions on the relative geometry between the trackers and the targets trajectory under which
L187@P1: the range information computed by the determinant of the
L188@P1: FIM is maximum.
L189@P1: (ii) We also propose an MPC-based tracker motion planning,
L190@P1: control, and estimation strategy that takes into account
L191@P1: the trackers’ constraints explicitly, in order to plan optimal
L192@P1: motions for the trackers to localize and pursue the targets.
L193@P1: In the MPC framework adopted, the control and planing
L194@P1: processes are based on the estimated information about the
L195@P1: target, thus making the approach more realistic than the
L196@P1: guidance law given in [13] where the targets’ motions are

L187: ## Abstract
L188: This paper addresses the navigation problem of automated guided vehicles (AGVs) in complex environments by proposing a collaborative trajectory optimization strategy based on the Set Membership Filter (SMF) and Model Predictive Control (MPC). In contrast, the traditional probability distribution-based navigation method, UKF-MPC, often fails to provide a strict safety margin when dealing with UBB noise, thereby increasing the risk of navigation failure.
L189: Therefore, this paper proposes a set-membership filter algorithm that constructs a minimum enclosing ellipsoid to enclose the system’s true state in real time and incorporates the geometric characteristics of this ellipsoid as a time-varying penalty term into the MPC optimization objective, thereby achieving dynamic risk avoidance. Finally, comparative experiments under three different types of environmental noise were conducted using MATLAB.
L190: The MATLAB simulation results indicate that, under complex environmental disturbances, the SMF-MPC control strategy exhibits a higher navigation success rate and greater robustness than both the traditional UKF-MPC control strategy and the Robust MPC control strategy.

L201: ## 1. Introduction
L202: With the deep integration of Industry 4.0 and smart logistics, AGVs have become indispensable core equipment in smart manufacturing systems, warehousing and logistics, and automated terminals [【75†1】,【76†2】]. In complex dynamic environments (such as high-density warehouses and human-robot collaborative workshops), AGVs must not only possess efficient path-tracking capabilities but also ensure extremely high navigation safety and robustness in the face of environmental disturbances [【77†3】,【78†4】].
L203: However, sensor measurement noise, mechanical transmission errors, and random disturbances caused by uneven surfaces—which are prevalent in real-world industrial settings—pose significant challenges to AGV positioning accuracy and trajectory control [【79†5】,【80†6】].
L204: Traditional AGV navigation and control frameworks largely rely on stochastic filtering algorithms based on probability distributions, such as the Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) and the Unbiased Kalman Filter (UKF) [【81†7】,【82†8】]. These methods perform well under the assumption that noise follows a Gaussian distribution [【83†9】].
L205: However, in real-world operating conditions, environmental disturbances often exhibit unstructured and time-varying characteristics, manifesting as UBB noise with unknown boundaries rather than an ideal Gaussian distribution [【84†10】,【85†11】].
L206: In such scenarios, probability-based filtering methods often fail to provide strict state estimation bounds, causing the system to potentially exceed its predefined range under extreme disturbances, thereby increasing the risk of collisions or even leading to navigation failure [【86†12】,【87†13】].
L207: MPC has been widely applied in the field of AGV motion control due to its ability to effectively handle system constraints and multi-objective optimization. In [【88†14】], the authors focused on solving the robust collision-avoidance formation navigation problem for a class of multi-unmanned surface vehicles and developed a novel controller based on distributed MPC to achieve collision-free formation navigation.
L208: In [【89†15】], a convex optimization model was derived to optimize dynamic feedback laws for linear systems subject to polyhedral uncertainty constraints, and a computationally efficient robust model predictive control law was defined.In recent years, researchers have attempted to combine UKF with MPC to enhance the controller’s robustness against disturbances by predicting the probability distribution of the state [【90†16】].
L209: In [【91†17】], a highly nonlinear dynamic environment was considered; since simple fixed-parameter linear controllers were unable to cope with the constantly changing dynamics and the various disturbance sources affecting the solar farm, a model predictive control strategy based on the UKF was designed and successfully applied in this field.However, when dealing with safety-critical tasks subject to strict hard constraints, such schemes struggle to mathematically guarantee that the system state remains within the safety domain at all times, due to the lack of an accurate description of state uncertainty [【92†18】,【93†19】].
L210: As a deterministic estimation method for handling UBB noise, the Set-Membership Filtering algorithm offers a new approach for navigation tasks with high safety requirements [【94†20】,【95†21】]. By constructing a minimal set that encloses the true state, SMF describes state uncertainty and provides the controller with a well-defined feasible state space.
L211: In [【96†22】], a set-membership filter is designed for all permissible unknown but bounded noise, such that the ellipsoidal set containing all possible states can be determined using a convex optimization method subject to probabilistic constraints. In [【97†23】], a new data-selective adaptive filtering algorithm—the Set-Membership Affine Projection (SM-AP) algorithm—was proposed.
L212: This algorithm demonstrates excellent performance in terms of convergence rate, final error, and reduced computational complexity, particularly when processing colored input signals. In [【98†24】], the distributed set-membership filtering problem was investigated for a class of time-varying multi-rate systems in sensor networks employing communication protocols.
L213: A set of distributed filters was designed, and the effectiveness of the proposed protocol-based distributed set-membership filtering algorithm was verified through numerical simulations. The aforementioned studies demonstrate that, compared to probabilistic filtering, SMF offers significant advantages in terms of robustness.
L214: Therefore, exploring a deep cooperative algorithm that integrates SMF and MPC, which transforms the geometric characteristics of state uncertainty into dynamic constraints for the control law, represents a key direction for enhancing the reliability of AGV navigation in complex environments [【99†25】,【100†26】].
L215: In response to the aforementioned challenges, this paper proposes a collaborative trajectory optimization strategy based on SMF-MPC. The main contributions of this work are as follows:
L216:   1. Kinematics and Noise Modeling: A kinematic model of the AGV that accounts for nonlinear characteristics was developed, and a refined UBB noise model was introduced to address disturbances in complex environments [【101†27】,【102†28】];
L217:   2. SMF-MPC Collaboration Framework: Existing SMF-MPC research has primarily focused on trajectory tracking problems. These studies typically treat the SMF’s estimated ellipsoid merely as a “more accurate single-point estimate,” without actively incorporating the ellipsoid’s geometric information into the MPC optimization objective. This paper provides a detailed derivation of the time update and measurement update algorithms for nonlinear ellipsoid membership filtering.
